t: Viral STIs: HIV, HSV, HPV and molluscum
sub: HIV integrates into host DNA, herpes hides in nerve ganglia and HPV grows in maturing skin cells, so each virus's life cycle predicts its tests, drugs and prevention.

pretest.q: Which HIV protein binds the CD4 molecule on a helper T cell?
pretest.why: The envelope protein gp120 binds CD4 and then a coreceptor, CCR5 or CXCR4. Only after that does gp41 unfold and fuse the viral envelope with the cell membrane.

w.gp41: gp41 is the envelope protein that causes fusion after gp120 has docked. Enfuvirtide blocks it, but it does not recognize the CD4 receptor itself.
w.p24: p24 forms the capsid inside the envelope, and fourth-generation tests measure it as an antigen. It never touches the cell surface, so it cannot bind CD4.
w.Integrase: Integrase is a pol enzyme that works later, inside the nucleus. It inserts the viral DNA into the host chromosome as a provirus.

pretest.q: Which enzyme must act first for acyclovir to become active?
pretest.why: Only the viral thymidine kinase, made in infected cells, adds acyclovir's first phosphate. Host kinases then make the triphosphate, which blocks viral DNA polymerase. This first step is what makes the drug selective.

w.Host guanylate kinase: Cellular kinases add the second and third phosphates, but they cannot start the process. This is why uninfected cells leave the drug inactive.
w.Viral DNA polymerase: The polymerase is the target that acyclovir triphosphate blocks at the end of the pathway. It is not the enzyme that activates the drug.
w.Reverse transcriptase: Reverse transcriptase belongs to retroviruses such as HIV. Herpes simplex is a DNA virus, and acyclovir does not act on this enzyme.

pretest.q: Which HIV marker becomes detectable first after infection?
pretest.why: Viral RNA turns positive on nucleic acid tests at about 10 days, before p24 antigen at 2 to 3 weeks and antibody at 3 to 4 weeks. This order is why fourth-generation tests, which include p24, catch infection earlier than antibody-only tests.

w.p24 antigen: p24 appears next, about a week after RNA. This is why an antigen/antibody test detects infection earlier than an antibody-only test, but later than an RNA test.
w.IgM antibody: Antibody of any class needs about 3 to 4 weeks to appear, because the immune system needs time to respond. So antibody-only tests miss the earliest infections.
w.IgG antibody: IgG is the last of these markers to appear, after 3 to 4 weeks. The antibody differentiation assay depends on it, so an RNA test is used when acute infection is suspected.

body: How do these viruses use the host cell and then persist?

Viruses are **obligate intracellular** parasites. A virus carries its genome and a few enzymes but has no ribosomes or energy supply, so it borrows the host cell's machinery. The STI viruses persist in different ways. HIV is a retrovirus: its {{rp17rt|reverse transcriptase}} copies its RNA into DNA, and **integrase** inserts that DNA into a host chromosome as a {{rp17prov|provirus}}. Resting CD4 cells that carry the provirus form a latent reservoir that no drug clears. Herpes simplex virus (HSV) is an enveloped, linear double-stranded DNA virus that, like other herpesviruses, takes its envelope from the nuclear membrane rather than the cell membrane. It has two phases. In epithelial cells it replicates actively, and the cells burst and release virus. In sensory neurons it enters **latency**, and its DNA sits as a circular episome. HPV also keeps an episome, in basal keratinocytes, and makes new virus only as those cells mature. Molluscum is a poxvirus that replicates in the cytoplasm of keratinocytes.

Each virus also evades the immune system in its own way. HIV mutates its envelope proteins, so antibodies lag behind, and it destroys the CD4 T cells that coordinate the response. HSV hides in neurons, where its latent genome makes almost no protein for T cells to see. HPV stays inside keratinocytes and causes little inflammation and no viremia, so the immune system barely notices it.
How does HIV enter, copy itself and deplete CD4 cells?

HIV has two copies of positive-strand RNA inside a cone-shaped **p24** capsid, wrapped in an envelope. Its three structural genes are gag (the p24 capsid and p17 matrix proteins), pol (reverse transcriptase, integrase and protease) and env. Env makes a gp160 precursor that a host protease cuts into **gp120**, which binds CD4 and then a coreceptor, and gp41, which fuses the envelope with the cell membrane. Early in infection the coreceptor is CCR5, on macrophages and memory T cells. Strains that use CXCR4 on T cells emerge later and predict faster decline. A person who is homozygous for the CCR5 delta-32 deletion lacks the coreceptor and resists CCR5-using virus, and heterozygotes progress more slowly. Reverse transcriptase does not proofread, so every cycle creates mutants. Mutations in env let the virus outrun antibodies, and mutations in pol select drug resistance.

Antiretroviral therapy (ART) is offered to everyone with HIV, whatever the CD4 count. It targets viral enzymes and proteins that human cells lack, so uninfected cells are largely spared. It always combines drugs, usually two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) plus an integrase inhibitor. A single drug would quickly select a resistant mutant. Host kinases activate NRTIs such as tenofovir, emtricitabine, abacavir and zidovudine. Their triphosphates lack a 3' hydroxyl, so they cause **chain termination** of the growing DNA. Tenofovir is already a nucleotide. Non-nucleoside inhibitors (NNRTIs) such as efavirenz bind reverse transcriptase at a separate, **allosteric** site and need no activation. Integrase inhibitors, the -tegravir drugs, block insertion of the provirus. Protease inhibitors, the -navir drugs, block cleavage of the gag-pol **polyprotein**, so virions bud but stay immature and noninfectious. Maraviroc blocks CCR5 and enfuvirtide blocks gp41, but both are used less often.

Kidney tubule injury and bone loss
Lactic acidosis, hepatic steatosis, pancreatitis, neuropathy
Maraviroc needs a tropism test; enfuvirtide causes injection-site reactions
Ritonavir is given for its side effect

Ritonavir is a protease inhibitor given at a dose too low to suppress HIV. Its job is to **inhibit CYP3A4**, the liver enzyme that clears most protease inhibitors. This raises the level and lengthens the half-life of the partner drug. Cobicistat boosts in the same way but has no antiviral effect. The cost is many drug interactions.
How is HIV diagnosed and staged?
Two to four weeks after infection, {{rp17ars|acute retroviral syndrome}} brings fever, rash, pharyngitis and lymphadenopathy. The viral load is enormous, but antibodies may not exist yet.
For years the patient feels well, but the virus keeps replicating in lymph nodes and the CD4 count slowly falls.
The CD4 count drops below 200 cells/mm³, or an AIDS-defining illness such as Pneumocystis pneumonia or Kaposi sarcoma appears.

Testing follows the CDC algorithm. A fourth-generation antigen/antibody immunoassay detects the **p24** antigen as well as antibody, so it turns positive earlier than an antibody-only test. A reactive result goes to an antibody differentiation assay, which separates HIV-1 from HIV-2. A negative or indeterminate result goes to an HIV-1 RNA test, which finds acute infection. The markers appear in a fixed order. RNA comes first at about 10 days, then p24 antigen at 2 to 3 weeks, then antibody at 3 to 4 weeks. The gap before antibody appears is the window period. The **viral load** measures replication and treatment response, while the CD4 count measures immune damage. Everyone is offered opt-out screening, and every pregnancy is tested.
How is HIV prevented, including from mother to child?

Prevention interrupts each route of transmission. Condoms block sexual spread, and sterile syringes prevent spread through blood. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (**PrEP**) is tenofovir with emtricitabine taken daily, or injected cabotegravir, by people at risk. Post-exposure prophylaxis (**PEP**) is a three-drug regimen for 28 days that must start within 72 hours of an exposure. Treatment also prevents spread: when ART keeps the viral load **undetectable**, the virus is not transmitted sexually. This is summed up as undetectable equals untransmittable.

Perinatal prevention follows the same logic. The mother takes ART during pregnancy. If her viral load is high near delivery, she receives intravenous **zidovudine** in labor and a scheduled cesarean delivery at about 38 weeks. The newborn takes zidovudine for several weeks. In the United States, formula feeding is still recommended because the virus passes in breast milk. As of 2025, however, federal guidelines support a mother on ART with a sustained undetectable viral load who chooses to breastfeed, after shared decision-making.
A newborn's positive HIV antibody test belongs to the mother

Maternal IgG crosses the placenta and can persist in the infant for up to **18 months**. So an antibody test in a baby born to a mother with HIV is positive whether or not the baby is infected. Infant infection is diagnosed with HIV **nucleic acid** tests, PCR for viral DNA or RNA, repeated over the first months of life.
Why does herpes keep returning, and how does acyclovir work?

Genital herpes, usually HSV-2 but increasingly HSV-1, causes painful grouped **vesicles** on a red base. They break into shallow ulcers. A first episode adds fever, painful urination and tender inguinal nodes. During that first infection the virus travels up sensory nerves and becomes latent in the **sacral** dorsal root ganglia. Oral HSV-1 settles in the trigeminal ganglion instead. Stress, menses, illness or immunosuppression can reactivate the virus, and silent viral shedding causes most transmission. Lesion PCR is the most sensitive test. A **Tzanck** smear shows multinucleated giant cells with Cowdry A inclusions, but it cannot tell herpes simplex from varicella-zoster. Blood tests for antibody are not used to screen people without symptoms.

Acyclovir is a guanosine analog that stays inactive until viral {{rp17tk|thymidine kinase}} adds its first phosphate. Host kinases then make the triphosphate, which blocks viral DNA polymerase and ends the DNA chain. Only infected cells contain the viral kinase, so uninfected cells are spared. Valacyclovir is a prodrug that is absorbed better, and famciclovir works the same way. High-dose IV acyclovir can form **crystals** in the kidney tubules, so patients are hydrated. Resistance, mostly in patients with AIDS, comes from a thymidine kinase mutation. **Foscarnet**, a pyrophosphate analog that binds DNA polymerase directly, treats resistant virus but damages the kidneys and lowers calcium and magnesium, which can cause seizures. Pregnant women with genital herpes take acyclovir from 36 weeks to lower the chance of lesions at delivery.
Why does acyclovir shorten a herpes outbreak but never cure the infection?

Acyclovir only works where viral DNA is being copied. It needs viral thymidine kinase to activate it, and its triphosphate blocks viral DNA polymerase. So it stops the burst of replication in skin and mucosa that produces vesicles and shedding. The latent virus in the sacral ganglia does none of this. It sits as a quiet episome in the neuron's nucleus, with no thymidine kinase and no polymerase activity for the drug to act on. When therapy stops, the next reactivation starts from that untouched reservoir. This is also why daily suppressive therapy reduces outbreaks only while it is taken.
How does HPV cause warts or cancer, and how are warts treated?

HPV is a nonenveloped virus with circular double-stranded DNA in an **icosahedral** capsid made of L1 and L2 proteins. It spreads by skin-to-skin contact, so condoms reduce but do not prevent transmission. It enters basal cells through tiny breaks in the skin. Infected cells become koilocytes, which are squamous cells with a wrinkled nucleus and a clear halo. Low-risk types 6 and 11 cause **genital warts**, the soft, cauliflower-like condylomata acuminata. High-risk types 16 and 18 cause cancers of the cervix, anus, oropharynx and penis. In these cancers the viral DNA integrates into the host genome, and the E6 protein degrades p53 while E7 inactivates Rb.

The 9-valent vaccine is made of {{rp17vlp|virus-like particles}} of the L1 protein. It covers types 6, 11, 16 and 18 plus five other high-risk types, and it is given at age 11 to 12. Because the particles contain no DNA, the vaccine cannot cause infection. Wart treatments remove lesions but not the virus, so warts often return.

**Molluscum contagiosum** is caused by a poxvirus. It produces firm, pearly, dome-shaped papules that are umbilicated, meaning centrally dimpled. Biopsy shows large eosinophilic cytoplasmic molluscum bodies, also called Henderson-Paterson bodies. The lesions clear on their own in healthy people, though curettage or cryotherapy can remove them. In adults the genital lesions are sexually transmitted, and widespread lesions suggest HIV with a low CD4 count.

body.q: Three weeks after a high-risk exposure, a man has fever, rash and a negative antibody-only HIV test. Which reasoning is correct?
o: A negative antibody test rules out HIV, because antibodies appear within days of any viral infection
Antibodies take weeks to form, but viral RNA and p24 antigen are already high, so an RNA test or antigen/antibody assay can detect acute infection
The CD4 count must fall below 200 before any HIV test turns positive, so testing should wait until symptoms of AIDS appear
Borrowed maternal IgG can hide adult infection for months, so the negative test reflects antibody from someone else
body.why: In acute HIV the virus multiplies explosively before the immune system makes detectable antibody, so an antibody-only test is negative during this window period. Viral RNA appears first, at about 10 days, and p24 antigen soon after. This is why antigen/antibody assays and RNA tests find infection weeks earlier. The CD4 count does not decide test results, and maternal antibody matters only in infants. His fever and rash are acute retroviral syndrome, when viral load is highest.
